questions.stem: Why are the heights of 200 students usually grouped into class intervals before graphing?
options: Grouping removes any outliers from the data set
There are many different values, so grouping shows the pattern
Grouping makes the data categorical rather than numerical
Heights must be grouped before their mean can be found
questions.explanation: Height is continuous, so 200 students may give almost 200 different values, and a graph of each value shows no clear pattern. Grouping into intervals such as 150 to less than 155 cm shows the shape. The data stay numerical.

questions.stem: A frequency table shows quiz scores: score 1, frequency 3; score 2, frequency 5; score 3, frequency 8; score 4, frequency 4. What is the mean score?
questions.explanation: Mean = (1 × 3 + 2 × 5 + 3 × 8 + 4 × 4) ÷ 20 = 53 ÷ 20 = 2.65. 2.5 averages the four score values without using the frequencies.

questions.stem: A frequency table shows quiz scores: score 1, frequency 3; score 2, frequency 5; score 3, frequency 8; score 4, frequency 4. What is the cumulative frequency for a score of 3?
questions.explanation: Cumulative frequency adds all frequencies up to and including that score: 3 + 5 + 8 = 16. 8 is the frequency of the score 3 alone.

questions.stem: A frequency table shows quiz scores: score 1, frequency 3; score 2, frequency 5; score 3, frequency 8; score 4, frequency 4. What is the median score?
questions.explanation: There are 20 scores, so the median is the average of the 10th and 11th. The cumulative frequencies are 3, 8, 16 and 20, so both the 10th and 11th scores are 3. 2.5 is the middle of the score values 1 to 4, which ignores the frequencies.

questions.stem: Times are grouped as 0 to 9 min (frequency 4), 10 to 19 min (6), 20 to 29 min (10) and 30 to 39 min (5). Using class centres, what is the estimated mean time?
options: 24.5 min
20.9 min
19.5 min
questions.explanation: Class centres are 4.5, 14.5, 24.5 and 34.5. Mean ≈ (4 × 4.5 + 6 × 14.5 + 10 × 24.5 + 5 × 34.5) ÷ 25 = 522.5 ÷ 25 = 20.9 min. 19.5 averages the four centres without the frequencies, and 24.5 is the modal class centre.

questions.stem: How does a histogram differ from a column graph?
options: A histogram cannot show the frequency of each value
A histogram shows numerical data with touching columns
A histogram shows categorical data with gaps between columns
A histogram always has columns of equal height
questions.explanation: A histogram displays numerical data on a continuous scale, so its columns touch. A column graph displays categories, such as favourite sport, with gaps between the columns.

questions.stem: How is a frequency polygon drawn on a histogram?
options: By joining the midpoints of the tops of the columns
By joining the top left corners of the columns
By joining the tops of the tallest and shortest columns
By drawing a line through the cumulative frequencies
questions.explanation: Each point is at the centre of a class interval at the height of its frequency, and the points are joined with straight lines. A line through cumulative frequencies is a cumulative frequency graph, a different display.

questions.stem: Which type of graph is best for showing how a household's spending is divided between rent, food, transport and other costs?
options: A sector graph
A line graph
A histogram
A stem-and-leaf plot
questions.explanation: A sector (pie) graph shows how a whole is shared among categories, as a fraction of the circle. A line graph shows change over time, and histograms and stem-and-leaf plots display numerical data.

questions.stem: Which display is best for comparing the test scores of two classes while keeping every score visible?
options: A back-to-back stem-and-leaf plot
A sector graph for each class
A divided bar graph
A single column graph
questions.explanation: A back-to-back stem-and-leaf plot shares one set of stems, with one class's leaves on each side, so the two distributions can be compared and every score can still be read. Sector and divided bar graphs show parts of a whole, not individual scores.

questions.stem: In a back-to-back stem-and-leaf plot, boys' times are on the left and girls' times on the right. One row reads 7 4 | 5 | 1 6 8. Which are the boys' times in this row?
options: 74 and 75
54 and 57
47 and 75
questions.explanation: The stem 5 is in the middle, and each leaf joins the stem to make a value: the left leaves 7 and 4 give 57 and 54. Left-side leaves are written outward from the stem, so they read right to left. 51, 56 and 58 are the girls' times.

questions.stem: A stem-and-leaf plot shows: 1 | 2 5 8, 2 | 0 3 3 7, 3 | 1 4 (stems are tens, leaves are units). What are the median and range of the data?
options: Median 22.6, range 12
Median 23, range 22
Median 20, range 22
Median 23, range 34
questions.explanation: The 9 values are 12, 15, 18, 20, 23, 23, 27, 31, 34, so the median is the 5th value, 23, and the range is 34 − 12 = 22. 22.6 is the mean, not the median.

questions.stem: In a survey of 180 students, 45 chose basketball as their favourite sport. What angle should the basketball sector have in a sector graph?
questions.explanation: Basketball is 45 ÷ 180 = 1/4 of the students, and 1/4 of 360° = 90°. 45° uses the number of students as the angle.

questions.stem: A divided bar graph 15 cm long represents 600 households. The section for households with solar panels is 4.5 cm long. How many households have solar panels?
questions.explanation: 4.5 ÷ 15 = 0.3, so 30% of the households: 0.3 × 600 = 180. 40 is the number of households represented by each centimetre, 600 ÷ 15.

questions.stem: A dot plot shows the values 2, 3, 3, 4, 4, 4, 4, 5, 5 and 9. Which features does it show?
options: A uniform distribution with no clusters or gaps
A negatively skewed distribution with an outlier at 2
A cluster from 2 to 5, a gap, and a possible outlier at 9
Two clusters of equal size, at 2 to 3 and at 4 to 5
questions.explanation: Most values are clustered between 2 and 5, then there is a gap with no values from 6 to 8, and 9 stands apart as a possible outlier. The values pile up on the left with a tail to the right, the opposite of negative skew.

questions.stem: What does it mean for a distribution to be positively skewed?
options: Most values are low, with a tail stretching towards high values
Most values are high, with a tail stretching towards low values
The values are spread evenly on both sides of the centre
Every value occurs with about the same frequency
questions.explanation: In a positively skewed distribution the data bunch at the lower end and the tail points to the right, towards higher values; incomes are a common example. A tail towards low values is negative skew.

questions.stem: A dot plot has two clear peaks, at 3 and at 8, with fewer values between them. How is the distribution described?
options: Uniform
Symmetric with one peak
Bimodal
Unimodal
questions.explanation: A distribution with two distinct peaks is bimodal, which often means two different groups are mixed in the data. Unimodal distributions have a single peak, and uniform ones have no peak.

questions.stem: A die is rolled 600 times and each face comes up close to 100 times. How is the distribution of results described?
options: Bimodal
Positively skewed
Multimodal
Uniform
questions.explanation: When every value occurs with about the same frequency, the distribution is uniform, and its histogram is roughly flat. Bimodal and multimodal distributions have distinct peaks.

questions.stem: House prices in a suburb are positively skewed by a few very expensive homes. Which measure of centre best describes a typical price, and why?
options: The mode, because house prices are categorical data
The range, because it includes the most expensive homes
The median, because the expensive homes have little effect on it
The mean, because it uses every price in the data set
questions.explanation: A few very high prices pull the mean upwards, so it overstates a typical price, while the median depends only on the middle value. Prices are numerical, and the range measures spread, not centre.

questions.stem: A column graph compares two brands' sales of 9600 and 10 000 units, but its vertical axis starts at 9500. Why is it misleading?
options: Column graphs cannot be used to compare two brands
The axis should start at the largest value, 10 000
The columns should touch, as they do in a histogram
The truncated axis makes a small difference look large
questions.explanation: Starting at 9500 makes one column 100 units tall and the other 500, so one brand appears to sell five times as much when the real difference is about 4%. The axis should start at 0 or clearly show a break.

questions.stem: An infographic shows a company's profit doubling by drawing a second coin twice as wide and twice as tall as the first. Why is this misleading?
options: Profit is categorical data, so it should not be drawn as a picture
A picture graph cannot be used for data that change over time
The larger coin has four times the area, so the rise looks bigger
The larger coin has twice the area, so the rise looks smaller
questions.explanation: Doubling both the width and the height multiplies the area by 2 × 2 = 4, and readers judge size by area. Only one dimension should be doubled, or the coins should be drawn the same size and counted.

questions.stem: Why can a three-dimensional sector graph mislead readers?
options: Three-dimensional graphs leave out the smallest category
Sectors at the front look larger than sectors of equal size at the back
Three-dimensional sector graphs can only show two categories
The angles of a three-dimensional graph must add to more than 360°
questions.explanation: Tilting the circle distorts the sectors, so slices nearer the viewer appear bigger than they are. A flat sector graph, labelled with percentages, shows the proportions accurately.

questions.stem: What is the mean of 4, 7, 9, 12 and 18?
questions.explanation: The sum is 4 + 7 + 9 + 12 + 18 = 50, and 50 ÷ 5 = 10. 9 is the median, the middle value.

questions.stem: What is the median of 3, 8, 5, 12, 7 and 10?
questions.explanation: Order the values first: 3, 5, 7, 8, 10, 12. With 6 values the median is the mean of the 3rd and 4th: (7 + 8) ÷ 2 = 7.5. 8.5 averages 5 and 12, the middle pair in the order given, without sorting first.

questions.stem: Using a calculator, what is the population standard deviation σ of 2, 4, 4, 4, 5, 5, 7 and 9?
questions.explanation: The mean is 5, and the mean of the squared deviations is (9 + 1 + 1 + 1 + 0 + 0 + 4 + 16) ÷ 8 = 4, so σ = √4 = 2. 2.14 is the sample standard deviation, which divides by 7 instead of 8.

questions.stem: Two classes both have a mean test score of 68. Class A has σ = 4.2 and Class B has σ = 9.8. Which statement is correct?
options: Class A's scores are more consistent than Class B's
Class B's scores are more consistent than Class A's
Class B did better overall, as its σ is larger
Both classes' scores are spread out equally
questions.explanation: A smaller standard deviation means the scores lie closer to the mean, so Class A's results are more consistent. σ measures spread, not performance, and the two means are the same.

questions.stem: Set A has mean 65 and σ = 5. Set B has mean 70 and σ = 15. Which statement is correct?
options: A has a higher centre, and its values are more spread out
B has a higher centre, and its values are less spread out
Both sets have the same spread, as their σ values differ by 10
B has a higher centre, but its values are much more spread out
questions.explanation: B's mean is 5 higher, but its standard deviation is three times A's, so B's values vary much more about its mean. A strong comparison mentions both centre and spread.

questions.stem: A shoe shop wants to know which size to order most of. Which measure of centre should it use?
options: The range
The standard deviation
The mode
The mean
questions.explanation: The shop needs the most common size, which is the mode. A mean size such as 8.37 may not even be a size that exists, and range and standard deviation measure spread.

questions.stem: A company says its mean salary is $140 000 to attract applicants. Most staff earn about $60 000, and a few executives earn over $1 million. Why is this an inappropriate use of the mean?
options: The mean can only be used for categorical data like job titles
The mean of a data set is always smaller than its median
A few very high salaries inflate it far above a typical salary
The mean ignores the executives' salaries completely
questions.explanation: The mean uses every value, so a few huge salaries drag it well above what most staff earn. The median would describe a typical salary far better.

questions.stem: What does a five-number summary list?
options: Mean, median, mode, range and σ
Minimum, mean, median, mode and maximum
Q1, Q2, Q3, IQR and range
Minimum, Q1, median, Q3 and maximum
questions.explanation: The five-number summary is the lowest value, lower quartile, median, upper quartile and highest value, which are exactly the five points a box plot is drawn from.

questions.stem: What is the five-number summary of 3, 5, 6, 8, 9, 11, 12, 15?
questions.explanation: The median of the 8 values is (8 + 9) ÷ 2 = 8.5. The lower half 3, 5, 6, 8 has median 5.5, and the upper half 9, 11, 12, 15 has median 11.5. 3, 5, 8.5, 12, 15 takes single values instead of averaging the middle pair in each half.

questions.stem: Why is the interquartile range often a better measure of spread than the range?
options: It is always larger than the range
It can be found without ordering the data
It is not affected by extreme values
It uses every value in the data set
questions.explanation: The IQR = Q3 − Q1 covers the middle 50% of the data, so one very high or low value barely changes it. The range uses only the two most extreme values, so a single outlier can change it a lot.

questions.stem: In a box plot, what does the box itself show?
options: The values within one σ of the mean
The middle 50% of the data, from Q1 to Q3
The lowest 50% of the data, up to the median
All the data except the outliers
questions.explanation: The box runs from the lower quartile to the upper quartile, with a line at the median, so it holds the middle half of the data. The whiskers reach out to the minimum and maximum.

questions.stem: A box plot has minimum 12, Q1 20, median 25, Q3 34 and maximum 50. About what percentage of the data are greater than 20?
questions.explanation: 20 is the lower quartile, and 25% of the data lie below Q1, so about 75% lie above it. 50% of the data are above the median, 25.

questions.stem: Parallel box plots summarise two classes' marks. Class A: minimum 40, Q1 55, median 62, Q3 70, maximum 85. Class B: minimum 30, Q1 60, median 68, Q3 74, maximum 90. Which statement is correct?
options: A has the higher median and the smaller IQR
B has the higher median and the smaller range
A has the larger IQR and the larger range
B has the higher median and the smaller IQR
questions.explanation: Medians: A 62, B 68. IQRs: A 70 − 55 = 15, B 74 − 60 = 14. Ranges: A 45, B 60. So B is higher in the centre and slightly more consistent in its middle 50%, but has the larger range.

questions.stem: In a box plot, the median is close to Q1 and the right whisker is much longer than the left. How is the distribution described?
options: Negatively skewed
Symmetric
Uniform
Positively skewed
questions.explanation: Values are bunched at the lower end and stretch out towards higher values, which is positive skew. A negatively skewed box plot has a long left whisker and its median close to Q3.

questions.stem: A dot plot shows the value 1 twice, 2 three times, 3 five times, 4 six times and 5 four times. What is the interquartile range?
questions.explanation: There are 20 values. Q1 is the average of the 5th and 6th values, (2 + 3) ÷ 2 = 2.5, and Q3 is the average of the 15th and 16th, both 4. IQR = 4 − 2.5 = 1.5. 4 is the range.

questions.stem: A data set has Q1 = 20 and Q3 = 34. Above what value is a data point an outlier, using Q3 + 1.5 × IQR?
questions.explanation: IQR = 34 − 20 = 14, so the upper limit is 34 + 1.5 × 14 = 34 + 21 = 55. 48 adds only one IQR, and 41 adds 1.5 × 14 to Q1 instead of Q3.

questions.stem: The data are 4, 6, 7, 7, 8, 9, 10, 11, 12, 25. Using Q1 − 1.5 × IQR and Q3 + 1.5 × IQR, which value or values are outliers?
options: 12 and 25
25 only
4 and 25
None of the values
questions.explanation: The lower half 4, 6, 7, 7, 8 gives Q1 = 7, and the upper half 9, 10, 11, 12, 25 gives Q3 = 11, so IQR = 4. The limits are 7 − 6 = 1 and 11 + 6 = 17. Only 25 is above 17; 4 is inside the lower limit.

questions.stem: The data are 4, 6, 7, 7, 8, 9, 10, 11, 12, 25. If the outlier 25 is removed, what happens to the mean and median?
options: The mean falls by about 1.7; the median falls by 0.5
The mean falls by 0.5; the median falls by about 1.7
The mean and median both fall by about 1.7
The mean falls by about 1.7; the median is unchanged
questions.explanation: With 25 the mean is 99 ÷ 10 = 9.9 and the median is 8.5. Without it, the mean is 74 ÷ 9 = 8.2 and the median is 8, the 5th of 9 values. The mean depends on every value, so the outlier affects it much more.

questions.stem: The data 1, 3, 4, 6, 6, 6, 8, 9, 10 have IQR = 5. A value of 22 is added. What happens to the IQR?
options: It stays at 5, as Q1 and Q3 both rise by 0.5
It rises to 21, as the maximum is now 22
It rises to 6, as Q3 now includes the 22
It falls to 4.5, as the median moves up
questions.explanation: Before: Q1 = 3.5 and Q3 = 8.5. After, with 10 values, the halves are 1, 3, 4, 6, 6 and 6, 8, 9, 10, 22, so Q1 = 4 and Q3 = 9, and the IQR is still 5. Q3 only depends on the middle of the upper half, not on how large the top value is.
